summary:
Space-App-X86 is an open-source 3D geospatial and Topological Data Analysis (TDA) platform built in Rust and WebAssembly, paired with the Planetary Settler desktop companion application in Rust and Java. Designed to bridge Earth-based field validation with planetary exploration, our system enables researchers and mission planners to compare terrestrial analog sites against candidate Lunar South Pole and Martian landing regions in real time.

Leveraging NASA open elevation and imagery datasets, including LRO LOLA, Mars MOLA, and JMARS, Space-App-X86 renders interactive split-view 3D terrain meshes alongside quantitative geomorphological metrics. By computing persistent homology invariants (Betti numbers β₀ and Euler characteristic χ), Terrain Ruggedness Index (TRI), Hypsometric Integral (HI), and real-time Landing Slope Hazard overlays (<5° safe and 15° critical thresholds), the platform objectively scores analog fidelity and identifies safe, traversable landing zones for future robotic and crewed missions.
details:
What It Does & How It Works:

Space-App-X86 is an open-source, dual-architecture platform for comparative planetary geomorphology and landing site assessment. It combines a high-performance Web & Native 3D/TDA engine built in Rust (Axum backend + Bevy WebAssembly/WebGL2 frontend) with Planetary Settler, an offline desktop companion application written in Rust and Java. Researchers and mission planners can load real 3D terrain meshes and Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) in a synchronized Split View to compare Earth analog environments (such as Lonar Crater, Atacama Desert, Mauna Loa, and McMurdo Dry Valleys) against candidate Lunar South Pole regions (Shackleton and Shoemaker craters, Connecting Ridge) and Martian landing zones.

The mathematical engine computes objective Topological Data Analysis (TDA) and geomorphological descriptors in real time: persistent homology Betti numbers (β₀ connected components), Euler characteristic (χ), Terrain Ruggedness Index (TRI), Hypsometric Integral (HI), elevation distributions, and dynamic Landing Slope Hazard maps (<5° safe landing threshold and 15° critical rover/lander hazard limit).

Benefits & Intended Impact:

Field testing rovers, landers, and astronaut operations on Earth requires proving that the selected terrestrial test site shares the true structural and topological roughness of the target extraterrestrial terrain. Space-App-X86 replaces subjective visual comparison with reproducible, quantitative topological fidelity scoring and slope-safety mapping—accelerating mission planning, reducing landing risk, and democratizing planetary terrain analysis directly in any modern web browser without requiring expensive proprietary GIS licenses.

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software:

- Languages & Frameworks: Rust (Axum, Bevy Engine, WebAssembly/WASM, Trunk), Java, HTML/CSS, and Fish/Bash shell automation.

- NASA Open Data & Planetary GIS Pipeline: NASA LRO LOLA (Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter), NASA Mars MOLA, ASU/NASA JMARS (for planetary albedo/imagery and 3D layer extraction), GDAL, QGIS, CloudCompare, and Blender (Blender-GIS).

- Hardware & Deployment Architecture: Distributed multi-node Linux workstation environment offloading Rust/WASM compilation and 3D mesh preprocessing over SSH to a dedicated Linux compute server, serving interactive WebGL2 clients over HTTP alongside local desktop execution via Planetary Settler.

Creativity & Key Factors Considered:

- Topological Invariance: Rather than relying solely on raw elevation differences, we applied persistent homology (β₀ and χ) so terrains can be compared by multi-scale structural connectivity (craters, ridges, and basins).

- Accessibility & Dual Workflow: Built a lightweight WASM web viewer with instant Guest Mode and Argon2id-authenticated Researcher Mode for cloud/LAN collaboration, paired with the offline Rust/Java Planetary Settler companion app for field environments without internet access.

- Engineering Safety Constraints: Incorporated lander stability thresholds (<5° nominal, >15° hazardous) and optimized mesh decimation/caching so heavy planetary DEMs render smoothly on standard student laptops.
